title: A Free AI Rebuilt Claude Code

lines.text: Last month, one single developer shook the walls of Adobe,
lines.label: Adobe shaken

lines.text: a company worth close to 100 billion dollars.
lines.label: Company value

lines.text: Photoshop, Premiere, all in just one week.
lines.label: One week

lines.text: He used about 8 Claude agents running at once.
lines.label: Eight agents

lines.text: But today, no paid Claude.
lines.label: No paid Claude

lines.text: We're doing the same thing with free open models you can run tonight.
lines.label: Free models

lines.text: Paste the setup prompt and run REA's health check until it passes.

lines.text: Today, a desktop app.

lines.text: everything the page downloads, and takes screenshots.

lines.label: 29 of 29

lines.text: Version 1.0.
lines.label: Version 1.0

lines.text: 77 out of 77 checks passing.
lines.label: 77 of 77

lines.label: 13-hour reset

lines.text: I switched to that model and typed: Read our files and saved versions.
lines.label: Resume work

lines.text: Check any unsaved changes and carry on where the work stopped.
lines.label: Check changes

lines.label: Not quite

lines.label: 77 to 102

lines.text: Every old test still passing.

lines.text: 25 new tests added and passing.
lines.label: 25 new tests

voice_script:
[curious] Last month, one single developer shook the walls of Adobe, a company worth close to hundred billion dollars. Photoshop, Premiere, all in just one week. He used about eight Claude agents running at once.

But today, no paid Claude. We're doing the same thing with free open models you can run tonight. We're not rebuilding Photoshop. We're rebuilding Claude Code itself.

An award-winning 3D website studied by the same free AI rebuilt in its own code and checked screenshot by screenshot against the real thing. [surprised] Somewhere in the middle, the free AI hits a wall. I'll show you the one line that gets you straight past it.

By the end, our free version goes head-to-head with the real Claude. Same task, same clock, one winner.

[thoughtful] Every AI coding tool has two parts. The body, the app you type into, and the brain, the AI model doing the thinking. Today, the body is OpenCode. The brain is DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Free. It will run out. When it does, we swap in GLM 5.3 Flash and carry on.

The third piece is REA, reverse engineer anything. 229 tools for looking inside software. Plug it into an AI and the AI becomes the detective. It doesn't copy code. It doesn't write code. It reads and reports back with proof. Understand the recipe. Don't photocopy the cookbook.

Install OpenCode, choose Windows x64, not ARM 64, and choose DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Free. Paste the setup prompt and run REA's health check until it passes.

Today, a desktop app. For native programs, REA needs a decompiler called Ghidra. The wrong version came first; the AI swapped in 12.1.4 and tested Notepad: 853 functions mapped. Green, 229 tools ready.

Before the big one, a warm-up. This is igloo.inc. It won site of the year at the awards. Can a free AI study it and rebuild it in its own code?

For websites, REA drives a real Chrome browser, reads the layout, the scripts, everything the page downloads, and takes screenshots.

[surprised] Error 429. OpenRouter's free models give you 50 requests a day for your whole account, and an AI agent burns through requests fast. So, I added Nvidia as a second provider, picked GLM 5.3 Flash, and typed one line: Carry on from where you stopped. It picked up exactly where it left off.

At one point, the AI proudly said, All 58 assets downloaded. I opened the folder: three files. So I sent one line back: Check the folder. Never say a file is saved unless a folder listing shows it. Try again. This time, 105 real files, 17.7 megabytes.

Read reverse.md and rebuild the site scene by scene in your own code. Never load the site's own JavaScript. Plain HTML and three.js, checking each scene in the browser before moving on. Then compare screenshots of the real site and our copy.

[thoughtful] The Claude app is the window. Claude Code is the engine inside that window. We're going after both, the window and the engine.

So, we changed the name, changed the icon, and this stays a private learning build, not for sale, not for release. I called it Kiln. The AI then writes its own code from scratch. Not one line of Anthropic's code makes it in.

Instead of repeating the same rules in every prompt, the AI writes them once into agents.md. Then there are three files: agents.md, the rules; features.md, our own engine and window; and spec.md, every feature, one test each, and a three-part build plan.

Then spec.md lands: every feature in the AI's own words, one test for each, and a plan in three parts.

The build prompt is: Read agents.md, spec.md, and our saved versions. Build the next unfinished part of the plan one feature at a time and test each one with the self-check.

The self-check drives the real Kiln window, types a message, and checks the file really got written. Kiln is not allowed to say anything works until that robot hand says pass. 29 out of 29 passed.

Then: Done. Version 1.0. 77 out of 77 checks passing.

Then DeepSeek ran out and wouldn't reset for 13 hours. I switched to that model and typed: Read our files and saved versions. Check any unsaved changes and carry on where the work stopped. Nothing lost because every finished feature was already saved into Git.

[skeptical] 77 out of 77 sounds perfect, right? It wasn't. The model picker wouldn't scroll. Four features were missing: /compact, helper agents, MCP servers, and hooks. The self-check only tests what the AI decided to build, not what it was supposed to build. Done is a claim. Check the receipt.

[confidently] One prompt fixed everything: Make the model picker scroll and add a search box. Then build what's missing: /compact, helper agents, MCP, hooks, and retry on rate limits, running the full self-check after each work. 40 minutes later, the self-check went from 77 to 102. Every old test still passing. 25 new tests added and passing.

Then I asked Kiln which model it was using. It said it wasn't powered by any separate large language model, which wasn't true. Now it knows its own brain.

Same task, same clock. On the left, the real Claude app. On the right, Kiln on a free model. Same empty folders. Build a simple todo app as one file called todo.html. Add tasks, remove them, delete one, refresh, and see how many are left. Which one would you keep?

One free app, one free brain, and REA. The free AI studied the Claude app and Claude Code, wrote its own blueprint, and built Kiln. Zero lines of code typed by me. [warmly] If you want more workflows like this, follow the channel.
